summary:
Delhi stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Human Rights Watch reported on 26 March 2026 that the bill removes the right to self-identification, limits recognition to those groups and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and creates offences of coercing or alluring a person that could criminalise the support systems trans people rely on. Human Rights Watch calls the bill a major reversal of hard-won rights and has urged the president not to sign it.

BBC News reported that the amendment bill has been approved by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, reversing the self-identification route established by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling. The government argues the narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted while strengthening protection against exploitation and trafficking. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel has asked the government to reconsider, citing privacy and dignity.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units. An estimated two million transgender people live in India, and the national documentation position is thin: the last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, of whom roughly 32,500 hold the identity cards required to access social security.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and trans people arrested by the force in Assam recounted degrading custody treatment in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters was documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The capital is the main stage for the dispute over the amendment bill. At a Delhi press conference, activist Grace Banu said the community sought "recognition without invasion" and "rights without humiliation", and rights campaigners including Akkai Padmashali describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Human Rights Watch's public appeal to the president and the Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel's request for reconsideration keep the bill's status in active contest.

The government's case rests on targeting rather than exclusion: it presents the narrower definition as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say the same definition excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. That contradiction, not a single provision, is what a visitor may see played out in encounters with officials.

The country's protection record is uneven by geography and institution. Courts have issued detailed, sweeping orders on police conduct and conversion therapy, while frontline enforcement bodies have generated the documented complaints. The UK Home Office's December 2025 assessment that police abuse is limited and not systemic sits alongside specific, named incidents at transport hubs and in custody.
localsOnly:
India's last census recorded 487,803 transgender persons, and only about 32,500 of them hold the identity cards described as essential for social security. That documentation gap falls hardest on residents, who must navigate medical certification to obtain recognition under the amended scheme.

Residents also face the pending shift in what recognition is available. Under the amendment, legal recognition is confined to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people self-identifying outside those categories fall outside the scheme, alongside the loss of the self-identification route set out in the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling.

The government states that a narrower definition will make welfare benefits, job reservations and healthcare support more targeted and will strengthen protections against exploitation and trafficking. Administrative and criminal consequences of the new coercion and allurement offences, and their effect on peer support and community networks, are set out by Human Rights Watch as a risk to the community's own support systems.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the amendment bill was still outstanding at the date of the BBC report; whether the bill has since been assented to, challenged, or brought into force is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Delhi-specific enforcement incident appears in the source inventory. The checkpoint and custody findings cited here were recorded at a railway station in Kolkata, in Assam custody in June 2024, at Chennai International Airport in November 2024, and in passport proceedings before the Allahabad High Court in February 2026; how far those patterns hold in Delhi specifically is not sourced.

The reference year of the census recording 487,803 transgender persons is not stated in the inventory, and the figure should be read as the most recent census count rather than a current estimate. The inventory separately gives an estimate of two million transgender people in India, and the relationship between the two figures is not resolved.

The specific penalties attaching to the new coercing or alluring offences are not stated in the sources available, nor is the effect of the medical certification requirement on passport or visa issuance for foreign visitors.
